stem: Choose the correct alternative and complete the sentence: In the swampy areas of Pantanal ______ are found.
solution: Correct alternative: hugo anacondas (printed thus; the intended word is 'huge anacondas'). The Pantanal, in south-western Brazil, is the world's largest tropical wetland. Its marshes and seasonally flooded grasslands are the classic habitat of the huge anaconda, the world's heaviest snake. The condor belongs to the Andes, the pink river dolphin to the Amazon river channels, and macaws to the Amazon rainforest canopy, so none of those three is the Pantanal-specific answer.

stem: Choose the correct alternative and complete the sentence: On the distribution of population ______ factor affects.
solution: Correct alternative: physiographic. Relief decides where people can live and farm — plains and river valleys carry dense population, while rugged mountains, deserts and dense forests remain thinly peopled. Sex-ratio, literacy and life expectancy are elements of the COMPOSITION or quality of a population; they describe the population, they do not decide where it settles.

stem: Choose the correct alternative and complete the sentence: The most common method of transportation in Brazil is ______.
solution: Correct alternative: roadways. Roads carry the bulk of both passenger and goods traffic in Brazil; the road network links the coastal cities with the interior and even reaches into the Amazon basin (for example the Trans-Amazonian Highway). Brazil's railway network is limited and mostly ore-carrying, waterways are important only along the Amazon and its tributaries, and airways, though well developed over such a large country, carry far fewer people than roads.

stem: Choose the correct alternative and complete the sentence: We should carry ______ for a field visit to collect information.
solution: Correct alternative: questionnaire. A field visit collects primary information, and a prepared questionnaire is the tool used to ask the local people planned, uniform questions so that the answers can later be compared and tabulated. A chair and a black board are classroom furniture; a water bottle is a personal need, not an instrument for collecting information.

stem: Choose the odd man out: Coastal states in Brazil.
solution: Odd man out: Acre. Rio de Janeiro (south-east), Paraiba (north-east) and Amapa (north) all border the Atlantic Ocean and therefore have a coastline. Acre lies in the far west of Brazil in the upper Amazon basin, sharing its border with Peru and Bolivia; it is completely landlocked and touches no sea, so it is the odd one out.

stem: Choose the odd man out: Region with very high rainfall in India.
solution: Odd man out: Western part of Rajasthan. The windward slopes of the Western Ghats, the Meghalaya plateau (Mawsynram and Cherrapunji) and Arunachal Pradesh all lie across the path of the moisture-laden monsoon winds and receive very heavy orographic rainfall, often above 200 cm. Western Rajasthan lies in the rain-shadow, parallel to the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon, and is arid with less than 25 cm of rain, so it does not belong to the group.

stem: Choose the odd man out: Tributary of river Amazon.
solution: Odd man out: Parana river. The Paru, the Purus and the Juruika (printed thus; the Jurua) are all tributaries that join the Amazon within the Amazon basin of northern Brazil. The Parana is not an Amazon tributary at all — it drains southern Brazil, flows south through Paraguay and Argentina and, joined by the Paraguay river, empties into the Rio de la Plata estuary in the Atlantic. It belongs to a separate drainage system.

stem: Choose the odd man out: Animals found in the Peninsular region of India.
solution: Odd man out: Yaks. The Indian bison (gaur), deer and antelopes (blackbuck, chinkara, nilgai) live in the forests and grasslands of the peninsular plateau. The yak is a high-altitude animal of the cold, treeless Himalayan and Ladakh plateaus, kept for milk, meat and transport above about 4,000 m; it cannot survive the heat of the peninsula, so it is the odd one out.

stem: Write a short note (any two of Q. 3): Retreating monsoon.
solution: Retreating monsoon: From about the middle of September the apparent movement of the sun shifts to the southern hemisphere, so the low pressure over north-western India weakens and pressure begins to rise over the land. The south-west monsoon winds therefore start withdrawing gradually from the north-west of India towards the south-east; by the end of December they have retreated from the whole country. The period of October and November is called the season of the retreating monsoon. Its features are: clear skies, high day temperature with high humidity giving oppressive weather known as 'October heat'; the withdrawal is gradual and irregular; low pressure develops over the Bay of Bengal and gives rise to tropical cyclones which strike the eastern coast, especially the Coromandel coast, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, sometimes causing great damage. During this season the north-east winds blow over the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and give rainfall to Tamil Nadu and the Coromandel coast, which is the main rainy season of that region.

stem: Write a short note (any two of Q. 3): Deciduous forests of India.
solution: Deciduous forests of India: These are also called monsoon forests and are the most widespread forest type in India. They grow in areas receiving between about 100 cm and 200 cm of rainfall. Their chief feature is that the trees shed their leaves for about six to eight weeks in the dry summer season to reduce loss of water by transpiration. They are of two types: (a) moist deciduous forests, in regions of 100-200 cm rainfall such as the foothills of the Himalayas, the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha, with trees like teak, sal, bamboo, shisham and mahua; and (b) dry deciduous forests, in regions of 50-100 cm rainfall on the interior of the peninsular plateau and the drier parts of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka, with trees like teak, tendu, palas, khair and babul. The trees have broad leaves, grow in pure stands and give valuable hard timber, so these forests are the most commercially useful forests of India; because they are easily accessible they have also been cleared most for farming and settlement.

stem: Write a short note (any two of Q. 3): Historical background of Brazil.
solution: Historical background of Brazil: Before the Europeans arrived, Brazil was inhabited by many native Indian tribes. In the year 1500 the Portuguese sailor Pedro Alvares Cabral reached its shores and claimed the land for Portugal, so Brazil became a Portuguese colony. The country took its name from 'pau-brasil', the brazilwood tree, whose red dye was its first export. The Portuguese set up large sugarcane plantations along the north-eastern coast and later coffee estates, and brought a very large number of slaves from Africa to work on them; this is why the population of Brazil today is a mixture of native Indian, European and African people. The discovery of gold and diamonds in Minas Gerais in the seventeenth century drew settlers into the interior. Brazil declared independence from Portugal in 1822 under Dom Pedro I and became an empire; slavery was abolished in 1888, and in 1889 Brazil became a republic. In 1960 the capital was shifted from the coastal city of Rio de Janeiro to the newly built inland city of Brasilia in order to develop the interior. Because of this Portuguese past, Portuguese is the official language of Brazil, unlike the rest of South America, which speaks Spanish.

solution: The Sao Francisco is the largest river lying entirely within Brazil. It rises in the Serra da Canastra in the state of Minas Gerais on the Brazilian Highlands, flows first northward through Minas Gerais and Bahia parallel to the Atlantic coast, then turns east near the border of Bahia and Pernambuco and empties into the Atlantic Ocean between the states of Sergipe and Alagoas. stem: Mark on the outline map of Brazil: Marajo island. Write its name and give the index.
solution: Marajo is the large river island lying in the mouth of the Amazon, in the state of Para in northern Brazil. It is bounded by the Amazon channel on the north-west, the Para river on the south and the Atlantic Ocean on the east, and lies almost exactly on the Equator, close to the city of Belem. It is one of the largest fluvial (river-formed) islands in the world and is famous for its seasonally flooded grasslands and buffalo rearing. On the outline map shade the island at the mouth of the Amazon on the northern Atlantic coast, write 'Marajo island' and add the shading to the index.

context: Mark the following in the outline map of Brazil. Write the names and give index (any four).
stem: Mark on the outline map of Brazil: Pampas. Write the name and give the index.
solution: The Pampas are the temperate grasslands of the far south of Brazil. In Brazil they cover the state of Rio Grande do Sul, in the extreme south, beyond the Tropic of Capricorn, bordering Uruguay to the south and Argentina to the south-west; from here the same grassland continues into Uruguay and Argentina. They have a moderate climate with rainfall of about 50-100 cm, soft nutritious grass, fertile soil, and are used for cattle and sheep ranching and for wheat. On the outline map shade the southernmost tip of Brazil, write 'Pampas' and show the shading with its meaning in the index.

solution: The Equator is the \(0^{\circ}\) parallel of latitude. It crosses Brazil through the northern part of the country, passing through the states of Amazonas, Roraima, Para and Amapa, very close to the mouth of the Amazon and through the city of Macapa. On the outline map draw a straight horizontal line across the northern part of Brazil, a little below the northern boundary and passing just north of the Amazon's mouth; mark it \(0^{\circ}\), write 'Equator' at its end and show the line symbol in the index. Because the Equator crosses the north and the Tropic of Capricorn crosses the south, most of Brazil lies in the torrid zone.

It was built in the interior deliberately, to draw population and development away from the crowded coast. stem: Give geographical reason (any two of Q. 5): Vegetation is scarce in the high altitudes of Himalayas.
solution: Reasons: (1) Temperature falls steadily with height, at about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 m, so the high Himalayas are extremely cold and the growing season is very short. (2) Above the snowline the ground is covered with snow throughout the year, so plants cannot root or grow. (3) The slopes are steep and rocky, the soil layer is thin, immature and poor in humus, so it cannot support big trees. (4) Strong, cold, dry winds blow constantly at these heights and dry up the plants. (5) The air is thin and oxygen is scarce. Therefore the tall coniferous forests give way to stunted alpine shrubs and short alpine grasses, and higher still only mosses and lichens survive, until beyond about 4,000 to 5,000 m the land becomes barren and snow-covered; that is why vegetation is scarce in the high altitudes of the Himalayas.

stem: Give geographical reason (any two of Q. 5): Tropical cyclones occur rarely in Brazil.
solution: Reasons: (1) The greater part of Brazil lies close to the Equator, where the Coriolis force caused by the rotation of the earth is almost nil; without it the rising air cannot begin to whirl, so a cyclone cannot form. (2) Along the Brazilian coast in the South Atlantic the surface temperature of the sea water usually remains below the 27 degrees Celsius needed for a tropical cyclone to be born, because cool currents move along that coast. (3) Strong vertical wind shear over the South Atlantic breaks up any storm that begins to build. (4) The South Atlantic lacks the easterly waves and the strong Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone activity that trigger cyclones over the North Atlantic, the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. For these reasons the South Atlantic is the ocean with the fewest tropical cyclones in the world, and Brazil is very rarely struck by one.

stem: Give geographical reason (any two of Q. 5): Settlements become sparse as we move towards the Amazon river basin.
solution: Reasons: (1) The Amazon basin is covered by dense equatorial evergreen rainforest (the Selvas), which is difficult to clear and to move through. (2) The climate is hot and oppressively humid throughout the year with very heavy rainfall of over 200 cm, which is unhealthy and uncomfortable for human beings. (3) The rivers flood over large areas and much of the land is marshy, so building and farming are difficult. (4) The hot wet climate breeds insects and diseases such as malaria and yellow fever. (5) The forest soil is leached and poor in nutrients, so agriculture cannot be sustained. (6) Roads and railways are few, so the region is inaccessible, and large parts are reserved as protected forest and tribal areas. Because of these unfavourable conditions people avoid the basin, and settlements become fewer and further apart as one moves into it.

stem: Give geographical reason (any two of Q. 5): Fishing plays an important role in the economy of India.
solution: Reasons: (1) India has a long coastline of about 7,517 km and a wide continental shelf together with a large Exclusive Economic Zone, which provide extensive fishing grounds. (2) The shallow, plankton-rich waters near the coast and the many creeks, lagoons and backwaters are excellent breeding grounds for fish. (3) India also has a large inland fishery in its rivers, canals, lakes, tanks and ponds, so fish are obtained in the interior as well. (4) Fishing gives employment and livelihood to lakhs of fishermen families along the coast, and supports allied businesses such as boat building, ice factories, canning and transport. (5) Fish is a cheap and important source of protein food for the people. (6) The export of fish and prawns earns valuable foreign exchange, and schemes of the Blue Revolution have further raised production. For all these reasons fishing is an important part of India's economy.

stem: Answer in detail (any two of Q. 7): Prepare a questionnaire for a field visit to a factory.
solution: A questionnaire for a field visit to a factory should contain short, clear questions arranged in order, for example: (1) What is the name and exact location of the factory? (2) In which year was the factory established and who owns it (private, government or co-operative)? (3) What articles are produced here, and what is the daily or yearly production? (4) Which raw materials are used and from where are they obtained? (5) What is the source of power used - electricity, coal, diesel or solar? (6) From where is water obtained and how much is needed? (7) How many workers are employed, and how many of them are skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled? (8) How many of the workers are local and how many have come from outside? (9) By which means of transport do the raw materials come in and the finished goods go out? (10) Where are the goods sold - local market, other states or exported? (11) How are the waste materials and effluents disposed of and what steps are taken to control pollution? (12) What safety measures and welfare facilities are provided to the workers? (13) What difficulties does the factory face and what help does it get from the government? At the end, thank the person who gives the information and note his name and designation.

stem: Answer in detail (any two of Q. 7): Give information of the coastal region of Brazil.
solution: Coastal region of Brazil: Brazil has a long coastline of about 7,400 km along the Atlantic Ocean, running from Amapa in the north to Rio Grande do Sul in the south. The coastal plain is narrow, especially in the south-east, where the Brazilian Highlands end abruptly in a steep escarpment called the Great Escarpment (Serra do Mar) that rises like a wall close behind the shore; in the north, near the mouth of the Amazon, and in the north-east the plain is broader. The coast has fine sandy beaches, sand dunes, bays and lagoons, the largest being Lagoa dos Patos in the south. The climate is hot and humid with good rainfall, since the south-east trade winds strike this coast. Because of the pleasant coastal climate, the fertile soil and easy contact with the sea, this is the most densely populated part of Brazil; most of its large cities and ports - Rio de Janeiro, Sao Paulo with its port of Santos, Salvador, Recife, Fortaleza and Porto Alegre - lie here. Sugarcane and coffee plantations, fishing, trade, industry and tourism (the beaches of Rio de Janeiro and the Copacabana) are the main occupations, so the coastal region is the economic heart of Brazil.

stem: Answer in detail (any two of Q. 7): Which factors affect the distribution of population of India?
solution: The distribution of population in India is affected by both natural and human factors. Natural factors: (1) Physiography - level plains and river valleys such as the Ganga plain are densely populated, while the rugged Himalayas, the Thar desert and the thickly forested hilly areas are sparsely populated. (2) Climate - regions with a moderate, pleasant climate and adequate rainfall attract people, while very hot deserts, very cold mountains and areas of excessive rainfall repel them. (3) Soil - fertile alluvial and black soils support intensive agriculture and hence dense population, while infertile and rocky soils do not. (4) Availability of water - people gather along rivers, canals and lakes, since water is needed for drinking, farming and industry. (5) Minerals - the mineral belt of Chhotanagpur has attracted population through mining. Human factors: (6) Industrialisation and employment - industrial centres such as Mumbai, Pune, Delhi, Chennai and Kolkata draw people from far away. (7) Urbanisation and migration - cities offer jobs, education, health care and better amenities, so they grow rapidly. (8) Transport and communication - well connected areas develop faster and become crowded, while remote areas remain thinly peopled. (9) Historical, social and political factors - old settled regions, government policies and the security of a region also influence where people live. As a result the density of population in India varies greatly, from over 1,000 persons per square kilometre in Bihar and West Bengal to fewer than 20 in Arunachal Pradesh.
